fields.v: Loop Engineering (version Not stated) with five loops: Issue Planner, Approved Builder, Preview Guardian, Test Release Controller, Master Reconciler. Coding agent and model Not stated ('command-line coding agents', 'multiple coding-agent generations')

Versioned scoped plan (plan record per issue); loop contract per loop (trigger, context projection, authority, verifier, stop, write-back); version-controlled Skills as procedural contracts (when applies, sources to read, tools, allowed changes, evidence, stop conditions); durable GitHub marker records (plan, phase/lease, review ledger, test lock, test evidence); consumable approval receipts bound to exact version; evidence records bound to head revision

Eligible issue -> Planner publishes versioned plan -> human plan approval -> Builder implements exact approved plan in isolated worktree, opens paired Preview/Master PRs -> Guardian reviews live PR head -> Test Controller locks exact SHA -> human exact-SHA test approval -> merge to test, deploy, runtime verification -> human-controlled production merge/release -> Reconciler. Any drift, ambiguity or missing evidence -> STOP / return to human

Plan gate (one exact plan version), test gate (one exact commit for test environment), production gate (master merge and production release human-only); humans also clarify intent and resolve ambiguous evidence
Full workflow in production (plan to test release); production path human-controlled

Spec-first (a versioned plan approved before implementation; Builder implements 'the exact approved plan'); authors' wording: 'versioned plan', 'procedural contracts'. Plan not maintained as source of truth after release (not stated)

rev.why: The approved artefact is a per-issue 'versioned, scoped plan' (pp. 3, 7) that the Builder must implement exactly; the paper never calls it a specification and does not say whether it is kept after release. Spec-first is defensible, but a reader could treat a task plan as not a specification and record 'not classifiable'.

fields.warn: O artefacto aprovado é um 'plano versionado' por issue, não chamado especificação. Decide se conta como spec-first ou se fica 'não classificável' (secções 3.3 e 4.2).
